title: The Winning of a Queen: Chapter 1
paragraphs: _I have told you how King Arthur won the excellent sword Excalibur to defend himself with. Now I will tell of many other noble and knightly adventures, through which he won a most beautiful and gentle lady to be his Queen._
_Everyone in the world knows the fame of the gracious Lady Guinevere. Yet I do not think the whole story of the adventures by which King Arthur won her good favor has ever been told._

_This tale tells of that courtship. It also tells of an enchanted disguise that King Arthur put on for his purpose, and of several adventures of daring knighthood that he undertook. So I hope that whoever reads what I have written will find it both pleasant and entertaining._
_How King Arthur Went to Tintagalon with Four of His Court, and How He Disguised Himself for a Certain Purpose._

One day King Arthur announced a great feast, to be held at Carleon upon Usk. Many noble guests were invited, and a splendid Court gathered at the King’s castle. At that feast seven kings and five queens sat in royal state. There were also high lords and beautiful ladies of rank, sixty-seven in number. And there were many of the famous knights of the King’s Court, who were counted the most renowned in arms in all of Christendom. Of all this great gathering of kings, lords, and knights, not one man looked unkindly at his neighbor, and all were united in good fellowship. So the young King looked around him and saw such peace and friendship among these noble lords, where before there had been quarrels and ill will. “Truly,” he said to himself, “it is wonderful how my reign has bound men together in kindness and good fellowship!” These thoughts lifted his spirit like a bird, and it sang within him.
While the King sat at the feast, a herald-messenger suddenly arrived from the west country. The herald came and stood before the King, and said: “Greetings to you, King Arthur!”
Then the King said: “Speak, and tell me, what is your message?”

The herald answered: “I come from King Leodegrance of Cameliard, who is in great trouble. This is how it stands. His enemy and yours, King Ryence of North Wales, is the same man who once insulted you by commanding you to send him your beard to trim his mantle. Now he makes certain demands of my master, King Leodegrance, and King Leodegrance is very unwilling to meet them. King Ryence of North Wales threatens to bring war into Cameliard because King Leodegrance will not give in at once. King Leodegrance no longer has the many knights and armed men he once gathered around him to defend his kingdom against attack. You, in your majesty, have brought peace to this realm and broken the power of all those kings under you. So the knights who once made King Leodegrance’s Court so famous have gone elsewhere. They seek better chances for their courage and skill at arms than his peaceful Court can offer. And so my master, King Leodegrance, begs help from you, who are his King and Overlord.”

King Arthur and all the Court that feasted with him listened to the herald-messenger in complete silence. The King’s face, which had been bright with cheerfulness, grew dark and clouded with anger. “Ha!” he cried, “this is truly no good news that you have brought to our feast. I will give your master, King Leodegrance, what help I can in this need, and I will do it quickly. But tell me, sir herald, what are the things that King Ryence demands of your master?”

“I will tell you, my Lord,” said the herald-messenger. “First, King Ryence demands a large part of the lands of Cameliard that lie along the borders of North Wales. Second, he demands that the Lady Guinevere, the King’s daughter, be given in marriage to Duke Mordaunt of North Umber, who is a relative of King Ryence. That Duke is a mighty warrior, but he is so ugly to look at and so violent in temper that I believe there is no one like him for ugliness or for madness of mood in all the world.”

When King Arthur heard what the messenger said, he was seized at once with a terrible rage. His eyes seemed to shoot out sparks of pure light, his face blazed like fire, and he ground his teeth together like the stones of a mill. Then he rose from the chair where he sat and left the place. All who saw his anger shuddered and turned their eyes away from his face.

King Arthur went alone into an inner room of the castle and walked up and down there for a long time. In all that time none of his household dared to come near him. The reason for the King’s wrath was this. Ever since he had lain wounded and sick, close to death, in the forest, he had kept in mind how the Lady Guinevere had suddenly appeared before him. She had seemed like a tall, straight, shining angel come down to him out of Paradise, full of pity and wonderfully beautiful. So the thought of that wicked, mad Duke Mordaunt of North Umber demanding to marry her filled him with a rage so violent that it shook his spirit like a mighty wind.
So for a long while he paced up and down in his anger, as I have said. No one dared come near him, but all stood far off and watched him from a distance.

After a while he gave orders that Merlin, Sir Ulfius, and Sir Kay should come to him where he was. When they had come, he talked with them for some time. He told Merlin to get ready to go on a journey with him. He told Sir Ulfius and Sir Kay to gather a large army of chosen knights and armed men, and to bring that army at once to the lands near the royal castle of Tintagalon, which stands close to the borders of North Wales and of Cameliard.

So Sir Ulfius and Sir Kay went to do as King Arthur commanded, and Merlin did so too. The next day King Arthur and Merlin set out for Tintagalon across the forest land of Usk. With them went certain famous knights of the King’s Court, the best proven in arms of all those around him. They were Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine, who were nephews of the King, and Sir Pellias and Sir Geraint, the son of Erbin.

They traveled all that day and part of the next, and nothing good or bad happened to them on the way. At last they came to the large and noble castle named Tintagalon, which guards the country bordering Cameliard and North Wales. Here King Arthur was welcomed with great rejoicing, for wherever the King went the people loved him dearly. So the people of Tintagalon were very glad when he came to them.

The morning after King Arthur came to Tintagalon, the summer night had been very warm, and he and Merlin were glad to get up early and go outside to enjoy the dewy freshness of the early day. In the cool of the morning they walked together in the garden, which was a very pleasant place, in the shadow of a tall, straight tower. All around were many trees with good shade, where the little birds sang sweetly in the cheerful summer weather.

There King Arthur spoke very freely to Merlin. He said: “Merlin, I believe the Lady Guinevere is the fairest lady in all the world. My heart seems always to be filled with love for her. I think of her all day long, whether I am eating, or drinking, or walking, or sitting still, or going about my business, and I dream of her many nights as well. It has been so with me, Merlin, ever since a month ago, when I lay sick in that hermit’s cell in the forest and she came and stood beside me like a shining angel out of Paradise. So I will not allow any other man but me to have her for his wife.

“Now I know very well that you are wonderfully skilled in the arts of magic that can change a man’s appearance, so that even those who know him best cannot recognize him. So I ask you very earnestly to disguise me, so that I may go into Cameliard unknown to anyone, and may live there in such a way that I can see the Lady Guinevere every day. I tell you truly that I want to see her in such a way that she does not know of my regard for her. I would also like to see for myself how great the dangers are that surround King Leodegrance, for the King is my good friend.”
“My Lord King,” said Merlin, “it shall be as you wish. This morning I will have you so disguised that no one in all the world will be able to tell who you are.”

That morning, a little before the first hour of the day, Merlin came to the King where he was and gave him a little cap. The cap was such that when the King set it on his head, he took on at once the look of a rough country fellow. Then the King ordered a jerkin of coarse frieze to be brought to him. He covered his royal and knightly clothes with it, and he hid the golden collar with its hanging jewel, which he always wore around his neck. Then he set the cap on his head, and at once he looked like a peasant farmhand.
Thus entirely disguised, he left Tintagalon unknown to anyone and went on foot to the town of Cameliard.

Toward the end of the day, as the sun was sinking, he drew near the place. He saw before him a large and important town of many pretty houses with red walls and shining windows. The houses of the town all sat on a high, steep hill, one above the other, and the town was surrounded by a great wall, high and strong. A great castle guarded the town, and the castle had very many towers and roofs. All around the castle were many fair gardens and lawns and meadows, and several orchards and groves of trees with thick and pleasant shade. At that time of day the sky behind the castle was one blaze of fire, so that the towers and battlements of the castle and its roofs and chimneys stood black against the bright light. Great flocks of pigeons circled the towers of the castle in constant flight against that fiery sky. King Arthur was tired from walking all day, and it seemed to him that he had hardly ever seen in all his life so fair and pleasing a place as that excellent castle with its gardens and lawns and groves of trees.
So King Arthur came to the castle of Cameliard in the disguise of a poor peasant from the countryside, and no one in all the world knew who he was.

When he reached the castle, he asked for the head gardener. When he spoke with the gardener, he begged to be taken into service in that part of the garden that belonged to the home of the Lady Guinevere. The gardener looked at him and saw that he was tall and strong and well built. He liked him very well and took him into service as he asked.
And that is how King Arthur of Britain became a gardener’s boy at Cameliard.

The King was very glad to be in that garden. In that pleasant summer season the Lady Guinevere came every day to walk among the flowers with her damsels, and King Arthur, disguised as a peasant gardener boy, saw her many times when she came there.
So King Arthur stayed at that place for more than a week. He did not mind that in all that time he enjoyed none of his kingly rank, but was only a gardener’s boy in the castle garden of Cameliard.

One day, when the weather was very warm, one of the damsels who attended the Lady Guinevere got up early in the morning, while the air was still cool and fresh. She left the Lady Guinevere still sleeping. This damsel, whose name was Mellicene of the White Hand, went into the ante-room, opened the window, and looked out into the rose garden that lay next to the Lady Guinevere’s bower.

In that place there was a carved marble figure of a youth, holding a marble pitcher in his arms. A fountain of water, as clear as crystal, flowed out of the pitcher into a marble basin. The figure, the fountain, and the marble basin lay in the shade of a linden-tree. All around was a thick growth of roses, so that the place was completely hidden, except from the windows of the castle high above.

So it happened that as the damsel looked down from the window, she saw a very wonderful sight. A strange knight was kneeling beside the fountain and bathing his face and chest in the crystal water. The damsel saw that the sunlight fell down through the leaves of the linden-tree and lay upon that strange knight. She saw that his hair and beard were the color of red gold, shining brilliantly in the bright morning. She saw that his brow and throat and chest were white as alabaster. And she saw that around his neck and shoulders hung a golden collar of marvelous beauty, so that when the sunlight shone on it, it flashed like pure lightning.

The damsel Mellicene saw this strange sight, which seemed like a vision, and stood for a long while entranced with wonder and delight. She did not know whether what she saw was a dream or not, nor whether the one who sat there was a spirit or a man of flesh and blood.

After a while she recovered somewhat from her astonishment. She drew back softly from the window, turned around, and ran lightly down the turret stairs, and so came out into the fair and blooming garden at the foot of the tower. She ran through the garden as fast and as quietly as she could. She came down a garden path to the marble fountain, the linden-trees, and the rose-trees where she had just seen that strange knight bathing in the crystal water.

But King Arthur had heard the damsel coming and had quickly put the cap back on his head. So when the damsel Mellicene arrived, she found no one by the fountain but the gardener’s boy. She asked him: “Who are you, fellow? And why do you sit here by the fountain?”
And he answered her: “I am the gardener’s lad who came a short time ago to work at this place.”

“Then tell me, fellow,” she said, “and tell me truly. Who was that young knight who was here beside the fountain just now, and where has he gone?” “Lady,” he said, “no one has been at this fountain today but me.”

“No, fellow,” she cried, “you are deceiving me. I assure you that I saw with my own eyes, just now, a strange young knight sitting here bathing in the waters of this fountain.” And the gardener’s boy said, “Lady, what I have told you is the plain truth, for no one has been here this morning but me. So if you think you saw anyone else, you are surely mistaken.”

At this, the damsel looked at him in great confusion. She was amazed, for she could not completely disbelieve him. Yet she could not fully believe him either, because her own eyes had seen what they had seen, and she knew she had not been mistaken. So she did not know what to think, and in her confusion she felt a deep anger toward that gardener’s boy. “Truly,” she said, “if you are deceiving me, I will make you suffer a great deal of pain, for I will have you whipped with cords.” Then she turned and left that place, still wondering at the strange sight and what it could mean.

That morning she told Lady Guinevere everything she had seen. But Lady Guinevere only laughed at her and teased her, saying she must have been asleep and dreaming when she saw that vision. In fact, the damsel herself had begun to think that this must be so. Even so, from then on she looked out of her window every morning, though she saw nothing for a long while, because King Arthur did not come back to that place soon.

Then, on another morning, she looked out of the window and, behold, the strange knight was sitting by the fountain once more, just as he had sat before. He bathed his face and his chest in the water as he had done before. He looked as handsome and as noble as ever, and his hair and his young beard shone like gold in the sun, as they had shone before. This time she saw that his golden collar lay on the edge of the fountain beside him, and it sparkled brilliantly in the sunlight while he bathed. After the damsel had watched him for some time, she ran as fast as she could to the room where Lady Guinevere still lay, and she cried out loudly, “Lady! Lady! Get up and come with me! That same young knight I saw before is bathing at the fountain under the linden tree right now.”
Then Lady Guinevere, full of wonder, got up very quickly. She dressed in all haste and went with the damsel to the window that looked out over that part of the garden.

There she saw the young knight herself, as he washed at the fountain. She saw that his hair and his beard shone like gold in the sunlight. She saw that his undershirt was of purple linen woven with gold thread. And she saw that beside him lay the skillfully made golden collar, set with many jewels of different colors, shining brilliantly where it rested on the marble edge of the fountain.

For a while she gazed at him in great astonishment. Then she commanded the damsel Mellicene to come with her, and she turned and went down the turret stairs and out into the garden, just as her damsel had done before. Then, as that damsel had done, she hurried as fast as she could along the path toward the fountain.

But when she arrived, behold, she found no young knight there, only the gardener’s boy, exactly as had happened with the damsel Mellicene before. For King Arthur had heard her coming and had at once put the enchanted cap on his head. Lady Guinevere was greatly amazed to find only the gardener’s boy, and she did not know what to think of so strange a thing. So she asked him, just as Mellicene had done, where the young knight had gone whom she had just seen at the fountain. And the gardener’s boy answered her as before: “Lady! No one has been at this place at all this morning, except me.”

Now when King Arthur put on his cap at the Lady’s coming, he had been in such a hurry that he forgot his golden collar. Guinevere saw it lying there, shining brightly, beside the edge of the fountain. “What is this!” she said. “Do you dare to make fun of me? Now tell me, fellow, do gardeners’ boys in the land you come from wear golden collars around their necks like the one that lies there beside the fountain? If I had you well whipped, it would be no more than you deserve. But take that trinket and give it to the one it truly belongs to. And tell him from me that it does not suit a true belted knight to hide himself in a lady’s private gardens.” Then she turned away with the damsel Mellicene, left that place, and went back to her chamber.

Yet all that day, as she sat over her embroidery, she kept wondering how that strange young knight could have vanished so suddenly and left only the poor gardener’s boy in his place. For a long time she could not solve the riddle.

Then, suddenly, at the hour when the heat of the day was giving way to the cooler part of the afternoon, she roused herself because a thought had come to her in an instant. So she called the damsel Mellicene to her and told her to go and tell the gardener’s boy to bring her at once a basket of fresh roses to decorate her tower room.

So Mellicene went and did as she was told, and after some time the gardener’s boy came carrying a large basket of roses. And behold, he was wearing his cap on his head. All the damsels who attended Lady Guinevere cried out at him when they saw that he wore his cap in her presence, and Mellicene of the White Hand demanded of him, “What! What is this, Sir peasant! Do you know so little of the respect owed to a king’s daughter that you wear your cap even in the presence of Lady Guinevere? Now I order you to take your cap off your head at once.”
And King Arthur answered her, “Lady, I cannot take off my cap.”
Lady Guinevere said, “And why can you not take off your cap, you rude fellow?”
“Lady,” he said, “I cannot take off my cap, because I have an ugly sore on my head.”
“Then keep your cap on,” said Lady Guinevere. “Just bring the roses to me.”

And so, at her command, he brought the roses to her. But when he had come close to the lady, she suddenly snatched at the cap and pulled it off his head. Then, behold, he was changed in an instant. In place of the gardener’s boy, there stood before Lady Guinevere and her damsel the figure of a noble young knight, with hair and beard like threads of gold. He let his basket of roses fall, so that the flowers scattered all over the floor, and he stood and looked at everyone there. Some of the damsels attending Lady Guinevere shrieked, and others stood frozen with amazement, hardly able to believe what their eyes saw. But not one of those ladies knew that the man they saw was King Arthur. Still, Lady Guinevere remembered that this was the knight she had found so badly wounded, lying in the hermit’s cell in the forest.
Then she laughed and threw his cap back to him. “Take your cap,” she said, “and go on your way, you gardener’s boy with the ugly sore on his head.” She said this because she meant to mock him.

But King Arthur made no reply to her. Instead, with a very serious face, he put his cap on his head again. Taking on his humble disguise once more, he turned and left that place, leaving the roses scattered over the floor just as they had fallen.

And after that, whenever Lady Guinevere came upon the gardener’s boy in the garden, she would say to her damsel, in a voice loud enough for him to hear, “Look! There is the gardener’s boy who has an ugly sore on his head, so that he must always wear his cap to hide it.”
She spoke openly like this, mocking him. But in private she told her damsels to say nothing about these things and to keep to themselves everything that had happened.
